paper_title: CausalAlign: Causal Alignment of Video Generation Models for Consistent Ego-Motion

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Diffusion-based video generation models (VGMs) can produce visually plausible videos, yet their camera ego-motion often drifts over long horizons. Camera ego-motion determines how the viewpoint changes between frames and is essential for maintaining consistent geometry and trajectories. To address this problem, we propose CausalAlign, a causal alignment framework with two components. First, we diagnose how precise ego motion is represented, used, and retained within VGMs using linear probes and causal interventions, revealing a rise-and-fall pattern during denoising. Second, we strengthen ego-motion state in VGM by aligning the representations at the identified layers to a 3D foundation model through delta-token space. This space encodes the changes between consecutive frames, allowing the alignment to focus on ego-motion dynamics rather than static scene content. With Wan2.2 fine-tuned on DL3DV and RealEstate10K, CausalAlign can largely improve motion accuracy, geometric consistency, and temporal smoothness, while preserving visual quality. For example, it improves geometric consistency by more than 20% relative to the base model. Moreover, with the fine-tuned VGM, CausalAlign improves the success rate of world action models (WAMs) by 10 points on mobile manipulation tasks of RoboCasa365 benchmark. Overall, CausalAlign improves ego-motion consistency in diffusion-based VGMs and yields noticeable gains in embodied models.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Recent advances in diffusion-based video generation models (VGMs) have led to remarkable models such as Wan2.2 (Team Wan et al., 2025) and Cosmos3 (NVIDIA Cosmos Team, 2026). Trained on Internet-scale collections of 2D videos, these models can synthesize visually compelling content (Huang et al., 2024, 2026). However, trained to model 2D appearance and local motion statistics, standard VGMs struggle to capture 3D camera trajectories and to control viewpoint changes consistently across frames (Wu et al., 2026; Kupyn et al., 2025). We refer to these cross-frame viewpoint changes as camera ego-motion. As shown in Figure 1 (left panel), prior work has attempted to address this challenge by introducing explicit 3D priors or preference alignment (Wang et al., 2024b; Ren et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025; Bahmani et al., 2025), yet generating videos with geometrically consistent camera trajectories remains an open problem. At the same time, recent work shows that VGMs can implicitly estimate camera poses from their internal representations, even when their generated trajectories are imperfect (Bahmani et al., 2025). This raises more fundamental question: how is precise ego-motion represented, used, and retained within VGMs? This question becomes increasingly important when VGMs are integrated into world action models (WAMs) for robotic mobile manipulation: visually plausible yet geometrically inconsistent predictions of the future can induce systematic errors in downstream action prediction. As the first step, we perform analysis for understanding the ego-motion information within VGMs. Inspired by prior works (Alain and Bengio, 2016; Meng et al., 2022), we adopt linear probing to measure the internal representations of VGMs and causal intervention to reveal the mechanisms of VGMs. Specifically, for linear 1 Figure 1: Overview of CausalAlign. Left: Existing approaches rely on external 3D caches that may propagate errors, optimize output-level preferences without directly supervising ego-motion states, or align 3D features at randomly selected layers. Middle: Our CausalAlign first identifies the targeted layers through causal diagnosis and then strengthens ego-motion states through delta-token alignment. Right: CausalAlign consistently improves camera ego-motion consistency in video generation and largely boosts downstream mobile manipulation performance. probing, we define decodability as the amount of ego-motion information. Meanwhile, for causal intervention, we define causal effect as the extent to which the interventions on VGM can change the generation. Our analysis results demonstrate that both measurements exhibit the same trend, that is, increasing first and then declining, across both denoising timesteps and denoising Transformer layers. These results suggest that ego-motion state emerges as the denoising progresses, however, fades away at the late timesteps and the last few Transformer layers at each step. Therefore, ego-motion is already learned and represented in VGMs, increasingly used at intermediate stages, yet not well retained at later stages. We refer to this progressive pattern as geometric state forgetting. Motivated by this diagnosis, our goal is to preserve and strengthen the ego-motion state within VGMs without compromising the quality of visual generation. To this end, we propose CausalAlign, framework with two components: causal diagnosis and delta-token alignment, as shown in Figure 1 (middle panel). First, causal diagnosis leverages linear probing and causal intervention to identify where ego-motion is represented, used, and forgotten within VGM. Second, delta-token alignment supervises the internal ego-motion state at the positions identified as forgetting. There are two key challenges in our alignment: how to represent ego-motion with the hidden states in VGMs, and how to provide meaningful geometry supervision for such representations. For the first challenge, we adopt the idea of delta tokens, which was initially designed for improving the eﬀiciency of the world model (Kerssies et al., 2026). We adapt this idea to measure the ego-motion via the difference between two consecutive frames. Delta tokens serve as natural carrier for motion information while reducing redundant static scene content. For the second challenge, we construct the delta-token space by leveraging the pretrained 3D foundation model. These 3D models are capable of estimating camera poses, depth, and 3D structure, and thus can provide high-quality geometric supervision. learnable projector then maps consecutive hidden-state transitions into this teacher delta-token space, explicitly supervising ego-motion state of the VGM. By aligning these projected tokens with the corresponding teacher delta 2 tokens at the identified layers, CausalAlign transfers geometric knowledge to the locations where ego-motion information starts to fade. With our CausalAlign method, we fine-tune the VGM on the widely-adopted datasets, DL3DV (Ling et al., 2024) and RealEstate10K (Zhou et al., 2018). To evaluate the effects of CausalAlign on VGMs, we establish comprehensive evaluation protocol with three aspects: visual quality, ego-motion consistency, and geometric state retention. Visual quality is measured with VBench-I2V (Huang et al., 2026) and complementary metrics. Ego-motion consistency is evaluated through motion magnitude, geometric consistency, and temporal dynamics, while geometric-state retention is assessed through probe decodability and causal intervention effects. CausalAlign preserves visual quality while improving camera ego-motion consistency, as shown in Figure 1 (right panel). For example, it reduces reprojection error by 22.6% and improves trajectory smoothness by 23.9% relative to the base model. It also alters the decodability and causal-effect patterns from rise-and-fall to rise-and-maintain, supporting the improved retention of ego-motion state. Moreover, we observe that the improved ego-motion state can facilitate downstream applications, such as WAMs for embodied tasks. Specifically, our fine-tuned VGM raises success rate on RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026) from 43.5% to 54.2%. These results validate our method with causal diagnosis and delta-token alignment. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We identify pattern called geometric state forgetting which reveals the ego-motion state in diffusion-based VGMs. Through linear probing and causal intervention, our analysis reveals that ego-motion information is progressively represented and used during the denoising process, yet not retained at the late stages of denoising. (2) We propose CausalAlign, causal alignment method that aims to preserve ego-motion state at the VGM layers identified by our causal analysis. Our technical innovation lies in adapting the idea of delta tokens to strengthen ego-motion consistency via 3D foundation models. (3) Extensive experiments and comprehensive metrics validate the benefits of our method. It largely improves ego-motion consistency, better preserves ego-motion state during denoising, and offers remarkable gains for WAM in robotic tasks.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Video diffusion and world action models. Video diffusion extends image denoising to joint spatiotemporal generation (Ho et al., 2022), while open backbones such as Wan have broadened its use (Team Wan et al., 2025). Unlike image generation, VGMs require preserving temporal correspondences and scene geometry across multiple frames (Huang et al., 2024, 2026; Ren et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). These priors increasingly serve as action-conditioned simulators or policies: Genie and IRASim learn controllable future dynamics, while VideoVLA, DreamZero, and LingBot-VA couple observations with executable actions; Fast-WAM shows that video co-training can improve action representations without test-time video decoding (Bruce et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026a; Yuan et al., 2026). Therefore, ego-motion consistency is internally related to WAM and erroneous camera motion can corrupt the predicted actions. Rather than proposing another WAM, CausalAlign restores and strengthens the ego-motion state of the VGM to facilitate WAM performance. Our method elicits the knowledge that has been learned during VGM pretraining, providing an alternative route for stronger WAMs. Feed-forward 3D foundation models. Feed-forward 3D reconstruction has progressed from point-map predictors such as DUSt3R and VGGT (Wang et al., 2024a, 2025a) to streaming models with temporal state. CUT3R recurrently maintains metric-scale scene representation (Wang et al., 2025b), while LingBot-Map organizes streaming context into anchor, pose-reference, and trajectory memories and demonstrates improved trajectory and pose accuracy over VGGT (Chen et al., 2026a). These models provide camera and scene representations that can serve as supervision for video generation. We thus adopt LingBot-Map as the teacher model and study how its ego-motion state can be transferred to video generator. Geometry-aware alignment and post-training. As summarized in Figure 1, existing geometry-aware adaptation methods can be categorized into three types. External 3D cache methods such as GEN3C and Voyager use point cloud or world memories for controllable camera motion, yet require additional geometric memory and may propagate cache errors (Ren et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025b). Preference alignment methods such as VideoGPA and Epipolar-DPO supervise generated videos through preference or epipolar 3 Figure 2: Three stages of CausalAlign training. CausalAlign transfers ego-motion knowledge from 3D teacher to the VGM through three-stage training. In Stage 1, consecutive features from streaming 3D foundation model are encoded into teacher delta-token space that captures inter-frame geometric transitions. In Stage 2, projector maps VGM DiT features into the same delta-token space and is frozen after training, using small subset of the training split. In Stage 3, with full training split, LoRA adapters are optimized only at the identified VGM layers using delta tokens, while the projector remains frozen. feedback, without directly improving the VGMs internal geometric state (Du et al., 2026; Kupyn et al., 2025). Direct alignment methods, including JOG3R, Geometry Forcing, and FantasyWorld, transfer geometric features into the generator but do not explicitly target at effective timestep and layer locations (Huang et al., 2025a; Wu et al., 2026; Dai et al., 2026). Complementary WAM methods leverage 3D, 4D, or action-grounded supervision to improve action representations without requiring auxiliary teachers at deployment (Li et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026; Qiu et al., 2026). CausalAlign instead improves the internal ego-motion state of VGMs through delta-token space from 3D foundation models, at the locations identified by causal diagnosis.

sections.title: 3.1 Method Overview
sections.content: CausalAlign combines causal diagnosis and delta-token alignment to preserve ego-motion representations in diffusion-based VGMs. We first conduct causal diagnosis to identify the layers and the denoising timesteps where ego-motion information fades. Guided by the causal diagnosis, we align the VGM using delta tokens in three stages. First, we learn delta tokens from frozen 3D foundation model. Second, we train projectors to map the temporal transitions of VGM features into this space. Finally, we use these tokens to supervise LoRA updates at the identified layers and denoising timesteps, while keeping the original VGM backbone, teacher, and projectors frozen. In this way, CausalAlign strengthens the geometric knowledge encoded in the VGM without introducing additional computation during video generation.

sections.title: 3.4 Inference
sections.content: At inference, CausalAlign follows the same video generation procedure as the original Wan2.2 (Team Wan et al., 2025). Given an initial frame and text prompt, the adapted VGM generates video through the standard denoising and decoding process. All auxiliary modules used during training, including the 3D foundation model, are no longer needed. Therefore, CausalAlign improves ego-motion consistency without requiring additional inputs or geometric computation during video generation.

sections.title: 3.5 Application to World Action Models
sections.content: Consistent ego-motion is important for mobile manipulation, where robots predict actions while their viewpoints change. We thus investigate whether improving the ego-motion state of VGMs can also benefit action prediction of world action models. Specifically, we initialize the video expert of Fast-WAM (Yuan et al., 2026) with our adapted Wan2.2 model. For the action expert, we follow Fast-WAM and transform the parameters of the original Wan model to initialize ActionDiT. We train both experts using the original objectives for flow matching: LWAM = Lv FM + La FM, (12) where and denote the video and action experts, respectively. The policy receives synchronized images from three camera views and predicts actions starting from the current observation. Future video is used as training target, while at inference, the policy predicts executable actions from the observed history without generating future video (Yuan et al., 2026). 6 Figure 3: Ego-motion diagnosis and retention. sections.title: 4 Experiment
sections.content: We first conduct causal diagnosis to identify where ego-motion information fades and examine whether CausalAlign improves its retention. We then fine-tune the VGM with delta-token supervision at these locations and evaluate its ego-motion consistency, visual quality, and the benefits for embodied tasks. Finally, we conduct ablation studies to validate our design choices.

sections.title: 4.1 Causal Diagnosis and Target Selection
sections.content: Setup. We freeze Wan2.2 (Team Wan et al., 2025) and diagnose the hidden states across Transformer layers and across denoising steps. At each location = (ℓ, s), linear readout predicts relative camera motion, yielding decodability score Dℓ,s. We also apply the causal interventions introduced in Section 3.2 and measure their effects on the generated camera trajectory, yielding causal effect score Cℓ,s. Figure 3 summarizes the resulting layertimestep profiles. Diagnosis and target selection. Both geometric decodability and causal effect in the original Wan2.2 exhibit consistent rise-and-fall pattern. Their increase at intermediate locations indicates that the VGM forms and uses an ego-motion state, while their subsequent decline suggests that this state is not retained during later denoising. By applying the target selection rule from Section 3.2, we select layers 14, 10, 12, and 20 in descending order of their layer-wise decline rates. Layer 14 is the primary target, while layers 10, 12, and 20 are auxiliary targets. The same rule applies to denoising timesteps {398, 799}. Both selected timesteps are used at all selected layers, with weights proportional to their positive temporal decline rates. The benefits of our method. After alignment, CausalAlign retains both probe decodability and causal effects at later denoising stages, changing the original rise-and-fall pattern into rise-and-maintain pattern, as shown by the orange curve in Figure 3. The sustained causal effects indicate that ego-motion information remains influential during generation, rather than merely becoming more decodable.

sections.title: 4.2 Experiments on the Comprehensive Evaluation
sections.content: Setup. We apply CausalAlign to Wan2.2-14B-I2V (Team Wan et al., 2025) and train it on datasets DL3DV (Ling et al., 2024) and RealEstate10K (Zhou et al., 2018). We choose these datasets since they provide camera pose annotations and cover diverse scenes and camera movements, making them suitable for supervising and evaluating ego-motion consistency. For each dataset, 90% of the data is used for training and 10% of the data is for evaluation. As in Figure 2, we first learn delta tokens from the geometric features of frozen 3D foundation model using 30% of the training data. We then train projectors to map features from the video generator into this delta-token space using 10% of the training data. Further details are provided in Appendix B.2. Baselines. We compare CausalAlign with the base model Wan2.2 and three groups of methods for improving geometric consistency. External 3D cache methods, including GEN3C (Ren et al., 2025) and Voyager (Huang et al., 2025b), control camera motion using explicit trajectories and 3D caches. We follow their standard inference procedures by providing the reference camera trajectory and constructing new 3D cache from the available input frames, without using future frames. Preference alignment methods, including VideoGPA (Du et al., 2026) and Epipolar-DPO (Kupyn et al., 2025), improve generated videos through preference or epipolar feedback. Direct feature alignment methods, including JOG3R (Huang et al., 2025a), Geometry Forcing (Wu et al., 2026), and FantasyWorld (Dai et al., 2026), transfer geometric features into the generator. For Wan2.2, CausalAlign, and methods without explicit camera control, we provide only the first frame and text prompt. Metrics. We use the same frozen estimators (Wang et al., 2025a) to recover camera poses, depth, optical flow, and visual features from every generated video. Our evaluation covers three complementary aspects. Motion Magnitude measures how closely the mean translational and angular speeds match the corresponding means from real validation videos (Appendix B.1). Geometric Consistency measures reprojection error (Triggs et al., 2000), consistency between depth and optical flow in static regions (Luo et al., 2020), and epipolar error (Lee and Civera, 2020). Temporal Dynamics measures trajectory smoothness and jerk (Hogan and Sternad, 2009; Flash and Hogan, 1985), capturing continuity of motion and abrupt changes in acceleration. Since the first frame and text prompt can admit several valid future camera trajectories, we measure intrinsic consistency rather than error against single reference trajectory (Appendix B.2). Further, its proximity to real camera speeds improves for both translation (0.68 to 0.79) and rotation (0.70 to 0.89), while epipolar error decreases from 2.9 to 2.1 pixels. sections.title: 4.3 Ablation Studies
sections.content: Semantic partitioning. We first investigate whether separating delta-token into motion, geometry, and visual information helps the model learn more effective representation. To this end, we compare our structured delta tokens, consisting of 64D ego-motion, 40D geometry, and 24D visual regions, with two unpartitioned 128D encoders. All encoders receive the same supervision, and we use PCA to project the unpartitioned representations to the corresponding dimensions. As shown in Table 4(a), our structured representation outperforms both alternatives across all six metrics. Further, the cross-probes in Appendix C.1 show that each region performs best on its corresponding task. These results suggest that explicitly separating different types of information helps the model learn more effective representations of ego-motion. Complete-space comparison. We next examine whether learning delta tokens provides advantages over directly using the raw features of pretrained 3D foundation model. We compare our 128D delta tokens with two representations from LingBot-Map: the concatenated features of consecutive frames (8192D) and their difference (4096D). Both original representations retain their full dimensions. As shown in Table 4(b), our delta tokens outperform both alternatives across all six metrics, despite using substantially fewer dimensions. For example, the rotation error decreases from 3.243 to 2.530 degrees compared with the original feature pair. These results suggest that learning compact representation of temporal changes is more effective than directly using the original pooled 3D features.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduce CausalAlign, causal alignment framework for ego-motion consistent video generation. By linear probing and causal interventions, we show that video generation models already learned and used egomotion state during denoising but did not retain it well at the late stages, pattern we call geometric state forgetting. CausalAlign targets at the locations where such forgetting is identified, and aligns ego-motion states with the delta-token space from 3D foundation model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CausalAlign consistently improves ego-motion consistency and temporal dynamics while preserving visual quality. It mitigates geometric state forgetting by changing the pattern of ego-motion state from rise-and-fall to rise-and-maintain. Further, our improved VGM largely raises the success rate of WAM on the mobile manipulation tasks of RoboCasa365. We hope this work can inspire the research on preserving geometric states of generative video models and the research on enhancing embodied models.

sections.title: Appendix
sections.content: The appendix provides details needed to interpret and reproduce CausalAlign. Appendix specifies the causal diagnosis, target selection, and three-stage delta-token alignment procedure, and provides additional evidence for geometric-state forgetting. Appendix defines the evaluation metrics and normalization, clarifies the training and trajectory protocols, and extends the experiments to text-to-video and camera-trajectoryconditioned generation. Appendix shows more ablation experiments to demonstrate the contributions of structured delta representations, update placement, temporal modulation, and auxiliary training objectives.

sections.content: A.1 Causal Diagnosis and Target Selection Diagnostic subset. We reserve fixed diagnostic subset Ddiag containing approximately 10% of the complete experimental data. The same subset is used to generate Fig. 3 and to select the target layers and denoising timesteps. Target selection is performed before adaptation using only the measurements from the frozen WAN2.2 base model (Team Wan et al., 2025). After adaptation, we re-evaluate the same subset only to visualize the change in the geometric state dynamics. The diagnostic subset is not used for the held-out evaluation or downstream WAM evaluation, and the selected target locations remain fixed in all subsequent experiments. Finally, we compare the geometry-commitment score K(s) of the evolving video latent with the internal ego-motion signals. B.2 Training and Inference Details We instantiate CausalAlign on WAN2.2-14B-I2V (Team Wan et al., 2025) using DL3DV (Ling et al., 2024) and RealEstate10K (Zhou et al., 2018). Each dataset is divided into 90% training data and 10% held-out evaluation data. Following the three-stage procedure in Fig. 2, the three stages use fixed 30%, 10%, and 100% subsets of the training split, respectively. 20 In Stage 1, the teacher delta-token modules, including the delta encoder, transition decoder, temporal predictor, and camera decoder, are trained with (38) In Stage 2, the VGM-side projectors are trained with Lmap while the VGM and all teacher modules remain frozen. In Stage 3, LoRA adapters are optimized only at λtemp = 0.1, λT pose = 0.2. where layer 14 is the primary target and layers {10, 12, 20} are auxiliary targets. The final objective is Ltar = {10, 12, 14, 20}, Star = {398, 799}, Lpose + λL, λ = 0.2. (39) (40) The original VGM backbone, LingBot-Map, teacher modules, and VGM-side projectors remain frozen during the final stage. Only the adapted VGM is retained at inference, and no teacher or external geometric cache is used. Why the main I2V protocol does not use direct ground-truth pose error. In the main first-frameand-prompt I2V protocol, the model receives only the first frame and text prompt. The future video is therefore one-to-many: multiple camera trajectories can be valid continuations of the same input. Directly comparing an unconstrained generated trajectory with single ground-truth trajectory can consequently penalize valid alternative motions. This differs from the causal diagnosis in Sec. 3.2. There, the ground-truth trajectory of the corresponding diagnostic video is used only as fixed measurement reference for Etraj(Y ; d). It is never provided to the generator. The diagnostic score measures how an intervention changes the generated trajectory error relative to norm-matched random control, thereby measuring the sensitivity of the generation process to the intervened internal state. It does not require the generated video to reproduce the reference trajectory. For the main unconstrained I2V evaluation, methods whose native inference does not require an explicit camera trajectory receive only the first frame and the text prompt. These methods are evaluated with matched output length, resolution, frame rate, sampling budget, and random seeds. For methods whose standard inference requires an explicit camera trajectory and 3D cache, such as GEN3C and Voyager (Ren et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025b), we follow their native inference interfaces: the ground-truth camera trajectory is provided as the camera-control condition, and fresh 3D cache is constructed from the available input frame(s), without using future video frames. These methods are reported as trajectory-conditioned baselines rather than as unconstrained generators. Regardless of the input interface, every generated video is processed by the same frozen, independent reconstruction pipeline. For the main intrinsic comparison, trajectory analysis is based only on the reconstructed video and uses motion magnitude, geometric self-consistency, temporal dynamics, and visual quality. Neither the conditioning trajectory nor its ground-truth trajectory is used as the target for these intrinsic metrics. Thus, the trajectory-conditioned baselines are not evaluated by ground-truth pose matching loss, while the evaluator and intrinsic metrics remain shared across methods. Results from unconstrained and trajectory-conditioned protocols are therefore interpreted separately. To complement this intrinsic evaluation, we introduce separate camera-trajectory-conditioned protocol. In this setting, the reference camera trajectory 1:T is provided as an explicit condition, and direct comparison with the target trajectory is well-defined. The results are reported in Sec. B.4. We next evaluate CausalAlign in two additional settings. The first tests whether the learned alignment transfers to text-to-video generation. The second evaluates direct trajectory accuracy under explicit camera conditioning. Within each setting, methods share evaluation inputs, output length, resolution, frame rate, sampling budgets, and evaluation procedures.
